prime.problem: The WaveNet lecture mixes three kinds of work: a new architecture, a rewrite of the code into torch.nn-style modules, and a string of silent bugs and small loss changes. Without a map it is easy to finish with a working tree net and no idea which change actually bought the improvement from val 2.1065 to 1.9937.
prime.fits: This card spans the whole course. It compresses the eight WaveNet cards into six claims, and it builds on the flat MLP from the MLP lecture and the BatchNorm layer (with its train/eval switch) from the BatchNorm lecture.
expect: modules and a Sequential container, and why BatchNorm needs a mode switch
fusing context in a tree whose receptive field doubles per level
batched @ and a view that turns pairs into a batch
a broadcasting bug that makes the loss slightly worse without an error
scaling up, the need for a harness, and convolutions as a speed trick
prime.goal: Draw the whole WaveNet pipeline from memory, with the shape on every arrow and the receptive field of every level, and say for each step of the performance log what changed and whether the log can prove it helped.

attend: Why does BatchNorm, and no other module in this lecture, need to know whether it is training or sampling?
What does the flat MLP do with 8 characters that the tree avoids, and where does each one's cost grow when the window doubles?
Which property of @ lets one Linear layer serve all 4 pairs at once, and what does a view have to do with it?
Why does the 3-D BatchNorm mistake raise no error, and what single fact about the tree's weights says the fix is right?
Which comparisons in the performance log are fair (same parameters, same steps), and which one never got run?
If a dilated convolution computes the same function as the loop, what exactly does it save, and when does it save nothing?

must: Each module owns its parameters and its forward step → Sequential chains them and collects parameters() → the architecture becomes one list → but BatchNorm keeps state and switches behaviour by mode → a forgotten training = False gives nan variance on a batch of 1 and poisons running_var

One flat Linear mixes all 8 characters at once and its first layer grows linearly with the window → fuse neighbours in pairs with one shared weight per level → the receptive field doubles per level (2, 4, 8) → context grows by one level per doubling instead of one giant layer

@ sums only over the last dimension → leading dimensions are batch → view(B, 4, 20) makes the 4 pairs a batch dimension for free → the same code leaves a position axis in front of BatchNorm → averaging over dim 0 only broadcasts silently into per-position statistics → reduce over (0, 1) (val 2.0265 → 2.0202)

Width 22,397 → 76,579 parameters takes val 2.0202 → 1.9937 but the train–val gap doubles (0.109 → 0.225) → one seed per row and no widened flat net → the log can't separate structure from size → you need a harness with equal-size controls and repeated runs
elevated: A dilated convolution slides the same tree over every position in one kernel and computes each shared node once (34 instead of 56 for the 8 rows of "diondre") → identical logits, lower cost → it only pays when many outputs come from one sequence, not from makemore's random minibatch rows
reference: PyTorch's nn.BatchNorm1d layout (N, C, L) vs the lecture's (N, L, C)
the lr schedule: 0.1, then 0.01 from step 150,000, 200,000 steps, batch 32

compress.prompt: Card closed, one sheet of paper: draw the whole WaveNet pipeline from memory. Start from a batch Xb of 8-character contexts, go through Embedding, three rounds of FlattenConsecutive(2) → Linear → BatchNorm1d → Tanh, and the output Linear, writing the shape on every arrow. Label each level's receptive field, mark where the training flag and the BatchNorm reduction matter, and write the performance log down the side, one line per change.
checklist: receptive fields 2, 4, 8, and one shared weight per level applied at every position
BatchNorm reduces over (0, 1) on 3-D input, and every layer's training is set to False before evaluating or sampling
the log: flat 3 chars 2.1065 → flat 8 chars 2.0342 → tree with the bug 2.0265 → fixed 2.0202 → wider 1.9937 (12,097 / 22,097 / 22,397 / 22,397 / 76,579 params)
a note that a convolution computes the same tree for every position and reuses shared nodes, changing cost, not outputs

retrieve.q: Explain, without code, why fusing 8 characters in a tree of pairs is a different model from feeding all 8 to one hidden layer, even when both have about 22K parameters.
answer: the flat layer combines every character with every other in one matrix multiply
the tree only ever combines two neighbours at a time, with one shared weight per level
information is built up gradually: 2, then 4, then 8 characters per node
at equal size they tied (notebook val 2.029 vs 2.027), so the structure alone didn't win here

retrieve.q: Walk a batch of 32 contexts through the first tree level of the 22K net (n_embd 10, n_hidden 68), naming every shape, and say what the buggy BatchNorm and the fixed one each store in running_mean.
answer: Embedding: (32, 8, 10); FlattenConsecutive(2): view as (32, 4, 20)
Linear(20, 68) via batched @: (32, 4, 68), the same weight on all 4 pairs
buggy x.mean(0): running_mean (1, 4, 68), 272 statistics from 32 numbers each
fixed x.mean((0, 1)): (1, 1, 68), 68 statistics from 128 numbers each

retrieve.q: You have one more hour of compute. Karpathy's log ends at val 1.9937 with 76,579 parameters. Would you spend it widening the tree further, or on something else? Justify with the numbers from the log.
answer: widening mostly bought train loss: train fell 0.142, val only 0.0265, and the gap doubled to 0.225
the log has no widened flat net, so it can't say whether the tree or the size won
one seed per row means small steps (the 0.0063 BatchNorm fix) might be noise
a better use: a flat control at ~76K, and repeated seeds of both, compared on val

retrieve.q: Your hand-written BatchNorm1d gets a 3-D input for the first time and training runs fine, but val is a little worse than expected. Which two mistakes from this lecture fit that symptom, and how do you tell them apart?
answer: reducing over dim 0 only: check running_mean.shape; (1, 4, 68) instead of (1, 1, 68)
forgetting training = False at evaluation: batch statistics are used instead of running ones
the second one is loud on a batch of 1 (nan, sampling crashes), the first never errors
print buffer shapes and the mode flag, not just the outputs

compare.q: Bengio's MLP and this lecture's tree both embed each character and run hidden layers. What is fundamentally different about how they combine the context, which design choice causes it, and when would you still pick the flat MLP?
answer: Bengio: concatenate all context embeddings and mix them in one hidden layer
tree: fuse neighbours two at a time, with shared weights per level, in log₂(context) levels
the choice is where mixing happens: all at once vs gradually
flat is simpler and was just as good at ~22K parameters here (2.027 vs 2.029); it gets expensive as the window grows (16,000 → 32,000 first-layer weights from 8 to 16 characters)

compare.q: The BatchNorm lecture already had a train/eval switch and running statistics. What new ways does this lecture find to get BatchNorm wrong, and why is one of them loud and the other silent?
answer: forgetting training = False: a batch of 1 has variance 0/0 = nan, so sampling crashes (loud)
the 3-D input reduced over dim 0 only: per-position statistics, broadcasting hides it (silent)
both come from BatchNorm depending on the batch, which no other layer does
the silent one costs only 0.0063 of val, so it is found by checking shapes, not by watching the loss

compare.q: The BatchNorm lecture already turned Linear, BatchNorm1d and Tanh into classes. What does this lecture's Sequential add, and what would still break if you kept a plain list of layers?
answer: Sequential runs the layers and collects their parameters in one object, so model(Xb) is the forward pass
it has the same interface as a layer, so containers nest
with a plain list, the training loop must gather parameters and flip every training flag itself
that is exactly the step where the nan sampling bug hides; torch.nn's model.eval() does it for you

predict.q: You want 32 characters of context. Keep n_embd 10 and compare the flat MLP (one hidden layer of 200) against the tree of pairs. Commit first: how many fusion levels does the tree need, and how many weights does the flat net's first layer have?
predict.answer: 5 levels, since 32 = 2⁵ and each level halves the number of nodes. The flat first layer takes 32 × 10 = 320 inputs, so it has 320 × 200 = 64,000 weights, doubling again from 32,000 at 16 characters. The tree's first level still sees only 20 inputs; each doubling of context adds just one more level. But the names are at most 15 letters long, so on this dataset most of those 32 slots would hold padding.

apply.task: Extend the lecture's final model (n_embd 24, n_hidden 128, 76,579 parameters) to block_size = 16 with a fourth FlattenConsecutive(2) level. By hand: write the shape after every layer for a batch of 4, then count the parameters and say where the new ones live. Then build it in your notebook, push a random (4, 16) batch through, print each layer's output shape and the total parameter count, and check both against your hand answer.
apply.hint: Only the new middle level adds weights: a (2·128) × 128 matrix plus its BatchNorm's 2 × 128. The embedding, the first level and the output layer don't change.
